activity_context.topic_title: Reducing a Quadratic Curve to Its Principal Axes

feedback.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $7{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+7{x}_{2}^{2}=1.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+7{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=1
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=9\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=5.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-9I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}]-9[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-9I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
